facts.value: £106.4m of borrowing at 31 December 2025 (p.2 narrative), against £30.2m of treasury investments. Appendix B (dated 30 September 2025) prints total £106,841,274.70 across 22 live PWLB loans (£76,601,274.70), six local-authority short-term loans of £5m each (£30,000,000) and one variable £240,000 arrangement with Folkestone Town Council. The £106.4m vs £106.84m gap is EIP amortisation between 30/09/25 and 31/12/25.

source.title: Appendix 7 — Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 — Council, 25 February 2026

facts.note: p.2 headline sentence. Appendix B on p.18 lists every loan with lender, rate, start and maturity. This is a favour to any reader — most councils do not publish loan-by-loan tables at this level of detail. Loan 714017 is listed at £0 (matured 22/03/2025) and loan 430141 is a £3,017.88 legacy annuity from 9 November 1973 at 11.38% — both are cosmetic tidy-ups, not stories.

facts.value: Appendix B shows 22 live PWLB loans totalling £76,601,274.70 at 30/09/2025. Derived weighted rate (Σ principal×rate / Σ principal from Appendix B) = 3.993%. Our PWLB price book at today (14 Aug 2026) shows 22 live loans totalling £75,901,923 — same count, £699k lower principal explained by ~10.5 months of EIP amortisation on the 7 EIP loans in the book.

source.title: Appendix 7 — Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 — Council, 25 February 2026

facts.value: £30m of LA short-term borrowing at 30/09/2025 from six different councils, taken between 15 July and 22 December 2025 (a five-month window): Portsmouth CC £5m at 4.22% (mat 13/08/2026), Milton Keynes CC £5m at 4.50% (mat 22/06/2026), East Sussex CC £5m at 4.25% (mat 14/07/2026), Northern Ireland Housing Executive £5m at 4.55% (mat 31/03/2026), Cornwall Council £5m at 4.50% (mat 13/10/2026), Brentwood BC £5m at 4.65% (mat 17/08/2026). Weighted 4.445%.

source.title: Appendix 7 — Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 — Council, 25 February 2026

facts.note: Six £5m tickets from six different councils in five months — that is an actively-worked LA market rather than a single big line. All six mature within a rolling twelve months from the balance sheet date. The strategy narrative on p.5 explains it: 'Short-term interest rates have fallen over the past year, and are expected to fall a little further, so it is therefore likely to be more cost effective over the medium-term to either use internal resources, or to borrow short-term loans instead.' Appendix A (22 Dec 2025) forecasts Bank Rate to 3.25% by mid-2026 — the strategy has short-borrowed against a rate-cutting view.

facts.value: Table 1 (p.3): Total CFR 156.8 (24/25 Actual) → 172.7 (25/26 Est) → 192.3 (26/27) → 203.4 (27/28) → 210.9 (28/29) £m. External borrowing (107.5) → (111.7) → (122.9) → (127.1) → (129.2). Internal borrowing 49.3 → 61.0 → 69.4 → 76.3 → 81.7. Balance-sheet identity ties exactly at every year on OLTL = 0.

source.title: Appendix 7 — Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 — Council, 25 February 2026

facts.value: Table 2 (p.4): Liability Benchmark 107.5 (24/25 Actual) → 122.6 (25/26 Est) → 150.1 (26/27) → 163.4 (27/28) → 175.9 (28/29) £m. External borrowing sits progressively BELOW LB in the forecast years: -£10.9m (25/26), -£27.2m (26/27), -£36.3m (27/28), -£46.7m (28/29).

source.title: Appendix 7 — Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 — Council, 25 February 2026

facts.note: The paper is explicit that sitting below LB is a live policy choice (p.4 narrative: 'Council, despite having an increasing need to borrow as defined by the Loans CFR, can manage this borrowing requirement using existing balance sheet resources (balances, reserves, cash flow surpluses) through what is known as "internal borrowing".'). The long-term chart (p.4) shows LB peaking around £215m in 2041. In outreach: note the shape factually only; do NOT frame it as under-borrowing.

facts.value: £30,205,894 of investments at 31/12/2025 (Appendix C, p.19). Composition: MMFs £16,540,000 across four funds (Aberdeen 5,000; Northern Trust 4,930; Federated 5,000; Goldman Sachs 1,610) at weighted 3.99%; CCLA Property Fund £5,087,195 at 5.42%; CCLA Diversified Income Fund £1,840,265 at 4.22%; Aegon Diversified Monthly £3,515,219 at 5.65%; Ninety-One Diversified Income Fund £3,223,216 at 4.39%. Overall yield printed at 4.73%.

source.title: Appendix 7 — Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 — Council, 25 February 2026

facts.note: Strategic pooled fund holdings total £13.666m against a £15m sector limit (Table 3, p.9) — well inside. The four pooled funds carry the IFRS 9 statutory override end-date of 31 March 2029 across the sector. The paper does not narrate the override cliff — worth mentioning as a training angle rather than a headline. MMF subtotal row prints 3.99% weighted yield but the four lines weight-average to 3.902% (9bp gap); rounding/basis, not a story.

facts.value: Not printed as a prudential indicator in this strategy paper. Financial Implications (p.14) states GF investment income 2026/27 £3.2m (£881k treasury + £2,360k Oportunitas/Otterpool loan interest) offsetting GF debt interest paid £3.2m — a broadly self-funding General Fund treasury position. HRA interest receivable £221k; HRA interest payable £2.9m — a £2.68m net cost against the £69.9m HRA CFR (implied ~3.83% average HRA borrowing cost).

source.title: Appendix 7 — Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 — Council, 25 February 2026

facts.note: The Financial Implications section is a paragraph, not the CIPFA financing-costs-to-net-revenue indicator table. A strategy paper (as opposed to an outturn) typically does not print the indicator itself. The £2,360k from Oportunitas and Otterpool on £98m Investment CFR implies an effective on-lending yield of ~2.41%, which is below the 3.99% weighted PWLB rate on the book. Structural spread compression — recorded for the file, not for outreach (§5).

facts.value: Authorised limit for borrowing £206m (p.5). Interest rate exposure: upper limit on one-year revenue impact of a 1% rise ±£280k (p.13). Maturity structure upper limits: under 12m 30%, 12-24m 40%, 24m-5y 50%, 5-10y 80%, 10y+ 100% (p.13). Long-term treasury investments (principal beyond year-end): £15m in each of 26/27, 27/28, 28/29; £20m no-fixed-date (p.13).

source.title: Appendix 7 — Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 — Council, 25 February 2026

facts.value: Appendix A (Arlingclose, 22 December 2025) forecasts Bank Rate at 3.75% current → 3.50% Mar-26 → 3.25% Jun-26 and flat 3.25% through Dec-28. 3-month money market rate 3.82% current → 3.30% from Jun-26 onwards. 10-yr gilt 4.52% current → 4.30% Sep-26 and marginally lower thereafter. 50-yr gilt 4.74% current → 4.60% from Sep-26 onwards.

source.title: Appendix 7 — Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 — Council, 25 February 2026

facts.note: Paper's own central case is a cut-and-hold path to 3.25% Bank Rate by mid-2026. Since the forecast was set, the DMO long-end curve has moved DOWN 40-70bp: 5-yr standard from 4.96% (implied Dec-25) to 4.38% (14 Aug 2026), 10-yr 5.52% → 4.87%, 20-yr 6.16% → 5.45%, 50-yr 5.74% → 5.34%. So the long end has overshot the forecast on the downside — favourable if new long-term borrowing is being considered. Short end has drifted higher than the forecast: 3.82% Dec-25 → 4.03% today for 1-yr, against a forecast path down to 3.30% by summer.

facts.value: Indicative discount on all 22 live PWLB loans as at 14 August 2026 (notice 314/26 PM): balance £75,901,923; settlement £73,523,949; net discount £2,377,974 (3.1% of principal). 18 loans below par, 4 above. Largest discounts on long-dated low-coupon PWLB: PW492233 mat 2054 4.05% −£423k; PW493698 mat 2055 4.55% −£361k; PW493914 mat 2053 4.55% −£345k. Largest premiums on recent higher-coupon: 796231 mat 2027 4.99% +£22k; PW488942 mat 2034 4.80% +£17k.

officer.body:
Hi,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on Appendix 7 (Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27) that went to Council on 25 February. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Appendix B — publishing the loan book at lender/rate/start/maturity level — is a favour a lot of councils don't do, and it's what let us check ourselves paragraph by paragraph.

A reconciliation first. Our PWLB file at today holds 22 live loans totalling £75,901,923 for Folkestone & Hythe. Appendix B (30 September 2025) prints 22 live loans totalling £76,601,275. Same count, and the £699k gap on principal is EIP amortisation on the seven EIP loans between the two dates. The £106.4m headline at p.2 ties to Appendix B's £106,841,275 within the same amortisation. Balance-sheet identity closes to the pound across all five years of Table 1 — 172.7 less 111.7 external less zero OLTL equals 61.0 internal for 2025/26, and analogous for every year through 2028/29. The paper doesn't print an overall weighted PWLB rate itself; from Appendix B it works out at 3.99%.

What's most distinctive is the £30m of short-term LA borrowing sitting on top of the PWLB book. Six £5m tickets from six different councils — Portsmouth, Milton Keynes, East Sussex, Northern Ireland Housing Executive, Cornwall and Brentwood — all taken in a five-month window from 15 July to 22 December 2025, at rates between 4.22% and 4.65% (weighted 4.44%), all maturing within twelve months of the balance sheet date. That's an actively-worked LA market rather than one big line. The p.5 narrative names the trade-off: short-borrowing against a rate-cutting view, with Appendix A's central case putting Bank Rate at 3.25% by mid-2026 and the 3-month money market rate at 3.30% from June onwards. The rolls across the next twelve months are where that view gets tested.

The other piece worth naming is the shape of the PWLB book. Priced against today's DMO premature-repayment curve, the 22 live loans sit an indicative £2.4m below par — around 3.1% net discount on £75.9m of principal. Eighteen are below par (mostly the 2007 and 2012 draws at 2.92-4.65%) and four are above (the recent 2023-25 EIPs and the 4.99% fixed from February 2025). That's what a book straddling the pre- and post-tightening eras looks like when the long-end curve has moved back down — 5-year standard from 4.96% at the paper's Appendix A date to 4.38% today, 10-year 5.52% to 4.87%. Every council's book is priced daily on this basis at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis, on the same DMO curve. Indicative only, and only the DMO can quote a real settlement; we model no MRP or accounting treatment on top.

One bit of wider context. July's sector PWLB drawings across all councils were £368m from just 19 borrowers — a thin month. The breakdown by tenor and by council is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity. And the current rate curve and the SONIA path it runs off are at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard. On our side we hold PWLB only, so the LA short-term line and the £240k variable with Folkestone Town Council aren't on our file — Appendix B is authoritative for those.

Four courses fit. Reading the PWLB certainty curve covers the mechanics of the Appendix A gilt+ margins. Liability Benchmark: the essentials is worth watching given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Code updates — Table 2 already prints the LB line at 122.6/150.1/163.4/175.9, which is ahead of many. IFRS 9 statutory override — the 2029 cliff matters for the £13.7m across CCLA Property, CCLA Diversified, Aegon Diversified and Ninety-One on p.19. And Short-term borrowing: the LA market from both sides fits the pattern in Appendix B. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
